newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UBS hopes NYC won't pass Holocaust bill.
newsitem.headline: UBS hopes NYC won't pass Holocaust bill.

text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) said on Wednesday it hoped New York City would reject a proposal to bar the city from putting money into Swiss banks until the Berne government sets up a Holocaust compensation fund.

UBS, the country's biggest bank, said recent efforts by Swiss banks to return lost Jewish accounts to their rightful owners meant there should be no reason for the New York City council to adopt the proposal.
"We would believe that if all the things Swiss banks have done in the recent past are taken into account in debating this proposal...it then may not pass," UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann said.
The two other biggest banks, Swiss Bank Corp and Credit Suisse Group, said they could not comment.
"It is too early. We must first study the proposals," said a spokesman for Credit Suisse, whose units include investment banking arm CS First Boston.

Under Jewish pressure, Swiss banks last year agreed to set up a joint commission with world Jewish groups and chaired by former U.S. central bank Paul Volcker to search for accounts left by Holocaust victims.
The banks last week also agreed in principle to a joint Holocaust memorial fund with the Swiss government and other businesses, although the amount and other details are still being worked out.
UBS declined to say how much business it did with New York City. "This is the kind of thing that falls under bank privacy," Erismann said.

New York's City Council Speaker earlier on Wednesday proposed a bill that would bar the city from depositing money in Swiss banks until the Swiss government established a compensation fund for Holocaust victims.
No estimate of how much money the city might have on deposit at such banks was immediately available, according to a spokeswoman for the Democrat-led City Council.
